chunks: ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Hāshim, from his father, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from some of our companions, from al-ʿAbd al-Ṣāliḥ (عليه السلام), who said:

The khums is from five things: from spoils, diving, treasures, mines, and salt-works. The khums is taken from each of these categories and assigned to those for whom Allah, the Exalted, has appointed it, while the remaining four-fifths are distributed among those who fought for it and administered it. The khums is divided into six shares: a share for Allah, a share for the Messenger of Allah, a share for the near relatives, a share for the orphans, a share for the poor, and a share for the stranded traveler. The share of Allah and the share of the Messenger of Allah belong, by inheritance, to those vested with authority after the Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وآله), so he has three shares: two shares by inheritance and one share apportioned to him from Allah; thus he has half of the complete khums, and the remaining half is for the people of his household. A share is for their orphans, a share for their poor, and a share for their stranded travelers; it is distributed among them according to the Book and the sunnah (prophetic tradition), in whatever suffices them for their year. If anything remains beyond them, it belongs to the wali, and if it falls short of their sufficiency, then it is upon the wali to spend from what is with him in the measure that suffices them.

It only became obligatory upon him to maintain them because what remains beyond them belongs to him. Allah made this khums specifically for them, to the exclusion of the poor among the people and their stranded travelers, as compensation for them in place of the charities of the people, as a purification from Allah for them due to their kinship with the Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وآله), and as an honor from Allah for them above the impurities of the people. So He assigned specifically for them, from Himself, that by which He enriches them so as not to place them in a position of humiliation and need. There is no harm in the charities of some of them being given to others among them. Those for whom Allah has appointed the khums are the relatives of the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وآله) whom Allah mentioned when He said:

They are Banū ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib themselves, their males and their females. No one from the households of Quraysh nor from the Arabs is included among them in this matter, nor are any of their clients included in this khums. The charities of the people are permissible for their clients, and they are equal to the rest of the people. Whoever has a mother from Banū Hāshim and a father from the rest of Quraysh, then charities are permissible for him and he has no share from the khums, because Allah, the Exalted, says:

The Imam has the select property: he may take from these properties their choicest part—the fine slave-girl, the fine riding animal, clothing, and goods—whatever he likes or desires. That belongs to him before distribution and before the extraction of the khums. He may also use that wealth to cover all the needs that fall upon him, such as giving to those whose hearts are to be reconciled, and other such matters incumbent upon him. If anything remains after that, he extracts the khums from it and distributes it among those entitled to it, and distributes the remainder to those responsible for that matter. If nothing remains after covering the public needs, then they have no share. Those who fought have no share in the lands, nor in what they overcame except what the army actually encompassed. The Bedouins have no share in the distribution even if they fought alongside the wali, because the Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وآله) made peace with the Bedouins on the basis that he would leave them in their homelands and they would not emigrate, provided that if an enemy incursion came upon the Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وآله), he would call them out and fight with them; yet they would have no portion in the spoils. His sunnah (prophetic tradition) remains operative regarding them and others.

The lands that were taken by force with cavalry and men are held in trust and left in the hands of those who cultivate, revive, and maintain them, according to whatever the wali agrees with them in proportion to their ability regarding the due—half, one-third, or two-thirds—in whatever amount is beneficial for them and does not harm them. When produce is brought forth from them, he begins by taking from it one-tenth of all that is watered by rain or flowing water, and half of one-tenth from what is watered by waterwheels and draught animals. The wali then takes it and directs it to the avenue that Allah has directed, over eight shares: for the poor, the needy, those employed over it, those whose hearts are to be reconciled, in freeing slaves, debtors, in the way of Allah, and the stranded traveler. These eight shares are distributed among them in their respective places according to what suffices them for their year, without hardship or stinginess. If anything remains from that, it is returned to the wali, and if it falls short and they are not sufficiently provided for, then it is upon the wali to maintain them from what is with him according to their means until they become self-sufficient.

After that, whatever remains of the tithe is taken and divided between the wali and his partners, namely the workers of the land and its cultivators. Their shares are paid to them according to the settlement made with them, and the remainder is then taken to serve as provisions for his aides in the religion of Allah and for the public interests incumbent upon him, such as strengthening Islam, strengthening the religion in the fields of jihad, and other matters in which lies the welfare of the public. None of that is for himself, whether little or much. After the khums, the anfal belong to him. The anfal are every ruined land whose people have perished, every land over which no cavalry or riding beasts were driven, but whose people made peace and surrendered with their own hands without fighting; the mountain peaks, the valley interiors, the thickets, every dead land with no owner, and the special properties of kings that were in their hands without usurpation, because all usurpation is to be restored. He is the heir of one who has no heir, and he supports the one who has no means.

He said: Allah has not left any category of wealth without apportioning it and giving every entitled person his due—the select and the general, the poor, the needy, and every category of people. He said: If justice were practiced among the people, they would become self-sufficient. Then he said: Justice is sweeter than honey, and none exercises justice except one who is proficient in justice. The Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وآله) used to distribute the charities of the desert-dwellers among the desert-dwellers, and the charities of the townspeople among the townspeople. He did not distribute among them equally into eight fixed portions such that each category necessarily received an eighth; rather, he distributed it according to those of the eight categories who were present before him, in proportion to what would sustain each class for its year. There is nothing in that fixed, specified, or formally set down; rather, he allocates it according to what he sees and what is present before him, until he fills the need of every group among them. If any surplus remained from that, the wealth as a whole was transferred to others.

The anfal belong to the wali, and every land opened in the days of the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وآله) remains so forever, as does what was opened through the summons of the people of tyranny and the people of justice, because the covenant of the Messenger of Allah for the former and the latter is one covenant. For the Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وآله) said: “The Muslims are brothers; their blood is mutually protected, and the least of them may uphold their covenant.” There is no zakat in the wealth of the khums, because the provision of the poor among the people has been placed in the wealth of the people over eight shares, so none of them remains unprovided for. Half of the khums has been assigned to the poor among the relatives of the Messenger (صلى الله عليه وآله), and that enriches them away from the charities of the people and the charities of the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وآله) and the wali al-amr. Thus no poor person remains among the poor of the people, and no poor person remains among the poor relatives of the Messenger of Allah (صلى الله عليه وآله) except that he has been enriched. Therefore there is no poor person, and for that reason there was no zakat upon the wealth of the Prophet (صلى الله عليه وآله) and the wali, because no needy poor person remained. Rather, there are obligations upon them arising from various directions, and for them from those same directions are corresponding rights.

key_terms.الْأَنْفَالُ: Non-military gains and designated properties reserved for the Imam.
key_terms.الْخُمُسُ: The one-fifth tax taken from specified categories of wealth.
key_terms.الْمَلَّاحَةِ: Salt-works as one of the sources from which khums is taken.
key_terms.الْوَالِي: The divinely vested authority responsible for administration and distribution.
key_terms.ذِي الْقُرْبَى: The near relatives of the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله entitled to a designated share.
key_terms.صَدَقَاتِ: Charitable alms, distinguished here from khums in eligibility.

ai.seo_question: How does this hadith explain the rules of khums, anfal, and the financial rights of Ahl al-Bayt?
ai.summary: This hadith lays out the legal framework of khums, fayʾ, anfal, and related public revenues, explaining their sources, allocation, and the authority of the Imam or wali over them. It also defines the entitlement of the Prophet’s near kin, distinguishes them from others regarding charity, and describes principles of public finance, land administration, and distributive justice in Islamic governance.
